newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels free hostage, govt says ready to talk.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels free hostage, govt says ready to talk.

text.p: Marxist rebels on Friday freed an ailing Peruvian security forces chief -- their first hostage release in 17 days -- as the government said it was ready to begin face-to-face talks to end the month-old standoff.

The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) freed Luis Valencia Hirano, head of the Delta special forces unit of the anti-terrorist police DINCOTE, for health reasons, at around 2 p.m. local time (1900 GMT).
Looking haggard and exhausted, Valencia pumped his fist in the air as he left the building to applause from the 73 remaining hostages.

"He was released so that he can resume his clinical treatment," said Red Cross mediator Michel Minnig, accompanying Valencia. He did not specify his medical condition but local media said Valencia had heart problems.

The release was followed by a brief statement from official negotiator Domingo Palermo stating that the government was ready to resume talks with the rebels but would not accept their main demand of freedom for about 400 of rebels' imprisoned comrades.
Palermo told a news conference arrangements had been made for him to meet MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini in a building near the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence.
Canada's ambassador -- among the first hostages to be released by the rebels -- would sit on a "guarantor" peace commission overseeing the talks, he added.
Although Palermo presented the meeting as definite -- adding that a Red Cross vehicle would transport Cerpa to the site -- it was not clear if the MRTA had agreed to it.
The rebels broke off a previously planned meeting with Palermo over the government's refusal to discuss their main demand.
"As is publicly known, the Peruvian state is not going to release the MRTA prisoners," Palermo said twice, to stress that the government was not shifting its position.
Earlier on Friday the mother of one of two girls among the roughly 15 MRTA rebels who stormed a cocktail party at the residence Dec. 17 arrived at the site to plead with her daughter to come out.
Emma Plasencia went to the 15th story of a nearby building to shout at her daughter, 16-year-old Giovana Vila Plasencia, to repent and give up.

Photographers on a roof overlooking the property said a rebel girl could be seen at an upper window of the diplomatic mansion talking to one of the hostages. It could not be verified if the girl was Plasencia.

MRTA international spokesman Isaac Velasco said the rebels would never surrender without achieving the liberation of their imprisoned comrades. He also blamed government inflexibility for prolonging the crisis.

"We have said it a million times, we will say it again. We will never give in," Velasco said at a news conference in the Danish capital Copenhagen. "The crisis will end when the Peruvian government decides it will and when it is willing to make a compromise," he said.

Velasco spoke after a day of sparring on Thursday, with the government rejecting an MRTA proposal that Guatemala be included in talks to end the crisis and the rebels slamming a decision to bar visits by the Red Cross and family members to the imprisoned MRTA rebels.

Peru's deputy Energy Minister Jorge San Roman celebrated his 57th birthday in captivity on Friday. Family members and colleagues marked the day by serenading him with a rendition of Elvis Presley's "Jailhouse Rock" from a street corner about a block from the residence.
In a rare piece of good news for Peru's President Alberto Fujimori, a major poll showed on Friday his popularity had increased significantly during the crisis.
Fujimori's approval rating rose to 50.3 percent in January from 44.9 percent in December, according to pollster Compania Peruana de Investigacion de Mercados (CPI).

The poll added that an overwhelming 93.2 percent of the population believed the president should look for a peaceful solution to the siege and 88.2 percent said no rebels should be released from prison.

The rebels have released more than 550 of the guests they originally seized at the diplomatic cocktail party. They have held onto those they consider the best bargaining chips including top government and security force officials, dozens of Japanese businessmen and diplomats and the younger brother of Fujimori.
